introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Why and with what consequences was the Berlin Blockade instituted between 1948 and 1949?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Berlin Blockade (24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949) was the Soviet closure of road, rail and canal links between the western zones of Germany and the western sectors of Berlin, which lay deep inside the Soviet zone. It was one of the first great crises of the Cold War. It was caused by disagreement between the Soviet Union and the Western powers about the future of Germany, and its consequences were the Berlin Airlift, the division of Germany and the hardening of the Cold War into rival blocs.

**1. Background.** At the end of the Second World War Germany was divided into four occupation zones (American, British, French and Soviet) and Berlin, the former capital in the Soviet zone, was likewise divided into four sectors under the Allied Control Council, as agreed at Yalta and Potsdam in 1945. The Soviet Union wished to keep Germany weak, to obtain large reparations and to protect itself from a revival of German power, while the United States and Britain came to believe that a revived German economy was needed for European recovery and that Soviet influence in Eastern Europe was expanding. The Truman Doctrine (March 1947) and the Marshall Plan (June 1947), which Stalin rejected for Eastern Europe, increased the tension.

**2. Reasons for the blockade.**
- *Western plans for West Germany.* The British and American zones were merged as the "Bizone" in 1947, and at the London Conference (February-June 1948) the Western powers, including France, agreed to unite their zones and prepare a West German government. The Soviets, who were excluded, regarded this as a violation of the Potsdam agreements and walked out of the Allied Control Council in March 1948.
- *Currency reform.* On 20 June 1948 the Western powers introduced a new currency, the Deutsche Mark, in their zones and extended it to West Berlin on 23 June. The Soviets feared that it would cause inflation and a flight from their own currency in their zone, and saw it as a step towards a separate West German state; they introduced their own currency in East Berlin.
- *Soviet aims.* Stalin wanted to force the Western powers to leave Berlin or to abandon the plan for a West German state, by using the city's isolated position as pressure. The Soviets claimed "technical difficulties" and stopped Western road, rail and barge traffic from 24 June 1948 and cut off electricity supplies from the Soviet zone. Berlin was also a symbol of the Western presence in the East and a centre of espionage; the Soviets wished to remove it.

**3. Course.** The Western powers did not leave and did not try to break the blockade by force, which would have risked war. The United States and Britain organised the Berlin Airlift (Operation Vittles and Operation Plainfare), flying food, coal and other supplies to West Berlin round the clock into the airfields of Tempelhof, Gatow and Tegel; over the months, more than two million tonnes of supplies were flown in. The West Berliners, led by their mayor Ernst Reuter, refused to give in. The West also imposed a counter-blockade on shipments of goods such as steel and coal from the western zones to the East. The Soviets did not interfere with the aircraft, and in May 1949 Stalin ended the blockade; the airlift continued for some months afterwards to build up stocks.

**4. Consequences.**
- *Failure of the Soviet aim.* The blockade failed and was a propaganda and political defeat for the USSR; the Western powers remained in Berlin and showed their commitment to its defence.
- *Division of Germany.* The crisis made the division of Germany permanent: the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) was created in May 1949 under its Basic Law (23 May 1949), with Konrad Adenauer as its first Chancellor, and the Soviets responded by creating the German Democratic Republic (East Germany) in October 1949. Berlin remained a divided city until the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961.
- *Military alliances.* The crisis convinced the Western powers of the need for collective defence, and led to the signing of the North Atlantic Treaty and creation of NATO on 4 April 1949; in the East the Soviet Union consolidated its bloc through Comecon (founded in January 1949) and, later, the Warsaw Pact (1955). The United States also stationed bomber aircraft in Britain.
- *Western unity and German attitudes.* The Western Allies and the Germans of the west came closer together, and West Germans, who had been enemies, began to see the Allies as protectors.
- *Hardening of the Cold War.* Europe was now divided into two hostile camps, mistrust grew, the arms race and the policy of containment were reinforced, and Berlin remained a focus of later crises (1958-61).

**Conclusion.** The Berlin Blockade was instituted because the Soviet Union wished to prevent the creation of a separate West German state and to force the Western powers out of Berlin after the currency reform of June 1948. It did not achieve those aims; instead it led to the Berlin Airlift, the creation of NATO and of the two German states, and an intensification of the Cold War in Europe.
